overall_summary: Analysis of 33 deduplicated Shorts reveals a stark polarization: extreme exoplanet and planetary phenomenon concepts consistently break out into high tiers (700-1,000+ views with high engagement), especially when framed via second-person immersion ('What If You Fell Into...') or mind-bending scale/weather contrasts. In contrast, generic psychology factoids (memory, earworms) and passive space trivia ('Why Space Is Completely Silent') suffer severe drop-offs and near-zero engagement. Recent performance shows sustained traction for immersive planetary survival and extreme astronomy scenarios.

winning_patterns.pattern: Second-person immersion into extreme planetary environments ('What If You Fell Into...')
winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,029 views, 38 likes, 2 comments), 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views, 18 likes), and 'What If You Fell Into the Darkest Planet?' (823 views, 15 likes) dominate performance.
winning_patterns.action: Use visceral physical consequences ('What happens to your body if...') paired with extreme planetary/astrophysical settings.

winning_patterns.pattern: Bizarre planetary paradoxes with high sensory contrast
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (1,029 views, 36 likes) and 'Venus Has a Day Longer Than Its Year' (981 views, 21 likes, most recent release) outperform standard space facts by 5x-10x.
winning_patterns.action: Select exoplanets or celestial bodies that defy basic earthly logic (e.g., temporal dilation, extreme atmospheric pressures, bizarre chemical states).

weak_patterns.pattern: Repetitive brain/psychology facts with generic 'mind blown' hooks
weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' uploaded multiple times yielded 5 to 53 views; 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' stalled at 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Retire generic neuroscience/psychology trivia unless framed as high-stakes micro-mysteries with cinematic visual pacing.

weak_patterns.evidence: Multiple uploads of 'Why Space Is Completely Silent' peaked between 34 and 220 views with minimal like ratios.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid passive explanatory questions ('Why is X...') in favor of dynamic visceral scenarios or tension-building hooks.

next_video.concept: Surviving a fall into Gliese 436b's gravity well where gravity compresses burning water vapor into solid hot ice (Ice-X) beneath an atmosphere that suffocates radar.
next_video.opening_direction: Macro visual rushing through glowing violet steam: 'If you dropped out of orbit over Gliese 436b, your heat shield wouldn't burn from friction—it would shatter against solid, superheated ice.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that despite surface temperatures reaching 800 degrees Fahrenheit, the immense gravitational force prevents water from turning to steam, locking it into an exotic crystal cage known as Ice X.
next_video.reason: Leverages the proven high-retention 'What If You Fell Into' formula and extreme astrophysics paradoxes that drive FACTVERSE's top views, but introduces an entirely fresh scientific phenomenon (Ice X / Gliese 436b) distinct from already-covered diamond, ruby, or dark planet titles.
fresh_topic_constraints: Do not repeat TrES-2b, 55 Cancri e, WASP-76b, HD 189733b, Venus, or Saturn's rings
Focus explicitly on exotic water states (Ice X / Ice VII under extreme compression)
Keep pacing tightly timed between 19 and 21 seconds with high contrast sound design

experiment: A/B test opening sentence format: Visceral physical action ('You drop through glowing purple clouds...') versus paradox statement ('Water boils at 212 degrees, but on this world, it freezes at 800') to test 3-second hook drop-off rates on high-concept astronomy.
